Munich massacre: 1972 Summer Olympics terrorist attack. The militants infiltrated the Olympic Village, killed two members of the Israeli Olympic team, and took nine other Israeli team members hostage.
Emerging in the 1970s among disillusioned liberal hawks, this political movement peaked in influence under George W. Bush and helped drive the push to invade Iraq in 2003 — what is it called?
Neoconservatism: Political movement of former liberals that combines political and social conservatism.
A Peronist who governed Argentina from 2003 to 2007, he later became the country's first 'first gentleman' when his wife succeeded him as president — who was he?

Néstor Kirchner: President of Argentina from 2003 to 2007. Néstor Carlos Kirchner Ostoić (25 February 1950 – 27 October 2010) was an Argentine lawyer and politician who served as the president of Argentina from 2003 to 2007.

One of the Three Kingdoms of Korea alongside Goguryeo and Silla, this kingdom in the southwest had the largest population of the three and was founded by Onjo near present-day Seoul. Which kingdom was it?
Paekche: Ancient Korean kingdom (18 BCE – 660 CE)
Considered the most influential artist of the Flemish Baroque, this painter and diplomat was known for dramatic, sensual compositions and designs for tapestry workshops — who is he?
Peter Paul Rubens: Flemish artist and diplomat (1577–1640)

Held every June in many cities to commemorate the 1969 Stonewall riots, this annual LGBTQ celebration of rights and self-acceptance began as marches in Chicago, New York, LA, and San Francisco in 1970 — what's it called?
Pride parade: LGBTQ celebration event. The events sometimes also serve as demonstrations for legal rights such as same-sex marriage.
Third pharaoh of the Nineteenth Dynasty, he waged 15 military campaigns and reigned 66 years — the longest recorded of any pharaoh — earning the title 'the Great.' Who was he?
Ramesses II: Pharaoh of Egypt from 1279 to 1213 BC.
An Italian neurobiologist who shared the 1986 Nobel for discovering nerve growth factor and served as a senator for life, she became the first Nobel laureate to turn 100 — who is she?

Serving as Ukraine's Defence Minister from 2023 to 2025 before becoming Secretary of the National Security and Defence Council, this Crimean Tatar politician has co-chaired a Crimea diplomatic initiative since 2020 — who is he?
The youngest person ever to hold the office, this Filipino politician became her country's vice president after serving multiple terms as mayor of Davao City — who is she?
Sara Duterte: Vice President of the Philippines since 2022.
The son of Ramesses I and father of Ramesses the Great, this Nineteenth Dynasty pharaoh ruled Egypt from around 1290 to 1279 BC — who was he?
Seti I: Egyptian pharaoh. Menmaatre Seti I (or Sethos I in Greek) was the second pharaoh of the Nineteenth Dynasty of Egypt during the New Kingdom period, ruling 1290 BC to 1279 BC.
Deported to Auschwitz as a teenager, she later championed France's 1975 law legalizing abortion and became the first woman to lead the European Parliament. Who was she?
A onetime Socialist who became a Macron advisor and helped launch En Marche!, this French politician later served briefly as Foreign Minister before joining the European Commission — who is he?
Stéphane Séjourné: French lawyer and politician (born 1985)
This Japanese politician served as Prime Minister from 2008 to 2009 and later became the longest-serving Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister in the country's history — who is he?
Tarō Asō: Prime Minister of Japan from 2008 to 2009. Tarō Asō (麻生 太郎, Asō Tarō; born 20 September 1940) is a Japanese politician who served as Prime Minister of Japan from 2008 to 2009.

Blaming rich families' land-grabbing for a supposed decline in Rome's population, this politician pushed an agrarian reform law to shift land to poorer citizens — and was killed for it in 133 BC. Who was he?
Tiberius Gracchus: Roman politician and social reformer (163 – 133 BC)

Known as the Risorgimento, this 19th-century movement folded numerous peninsular states into the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1861 and finished in 1871 when Rome became the new nation's capital — what was it?
Unification of Italy: 1848–1870 consolidation of Italian states.
This former heavyweight boxer holds a PhD and has served as the mayor of Kyiv since 2014 — who is he?
Vitali Klitschko: Ukrainian politician and boxer (born 1971)
Founded, by legend, by Cerdic and Cynric of the Gewisse, this Anglo-Saxon kingdom in southern Britain lasted from around 519 to 927 — what was it called?
Wessex: Anglo-Saxon kingdom in the south of Great Britain.
Son of Darius the Great and a grandson of Cyrus the Great, this Achaemenid King of Kings is best remembered for his doomed 480 BC invasion of Greece — who?
Xerxes I: King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire from 486 to 465 BC.
Nicknamed the 'Young Marshal' after his father's assassination, this Chinese general arrested Chiang Kai-shek in 1936 to force a united front against Japan — who is he?
Zhang Xueliang: Chinese general and warlord (1901–2001)
Who among these was born first?
Qian Xuesen (born 1911) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Levi Strauss (born 1829) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these was founded earliest?
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four has been around longest?
Earth (formed ~4.54 billion years ago) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these is an astronomer?
Frank Kameny is an astronomer. Franklin Edward Kameny (May 21, 1925 – October 11, 2011) was an American gay rights activist.
Pick the mathematician from these four.
Eugene Wigner is a mathematician. Wigner and Hermann Weyl were responsible for introducing group theory into physics, particularly the theory of symmetry in physics.
What is the atomic number of Seaborgium?
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Sg and atomic number 106.
What is the atomic number of Bromine?
Bromine is a chemical element; it has symbol Br and atomic number 35.
In what year was Abraham Maslow born?
Abraham Maslow: Maslow was a psychology professor at Cornell University, Brooklyn College, Brandeis University, The New School for Social Research, and Columbia University.
In what year was Larry Page born?
Larry Page: Lawrence Edward Page (born March 26, 1973) is an American businessman and computer scientist who co-founded Google with Sergey Brin.
In what year was Alexey Pajitnov born?
Alexey Pajitnov: Alexey Leonidovich Pajitnov (born April 16, 1955) is a Russian and American computer engineer and video game designer.
In what year did Omar Khayyam die?
Omar Khayyam (1048–1131) was a Persian poet and polymath, known for his contributions to mathematics, astronomy, philosophy, and Persian literature.
In what year did James Clerk Maxwell die?
James Clerk Maxwell: Maxwell's equations for electromagnetism achieved the second great unification in physics, where the first one had been realised by Isaac Newton.
In what year was Sodium discovered?
Sodium is a chemical element; it has symbol Na (from Neo-Latin natrium) and atomic number 11.
Ammonium chloride: Pfizer. Ammonium chloride is an inorganic chemical compound with the chemical formula NH4Cl, also written as [NH4]Cl.
In which country is Embraer E-Jet E2 family based?
Embraer E-Jet E2 family: Brazil. The Embraer E-Jet E2 family is a series of four-abreast narrow-body regional jet airliners designed and produced by the Brazilian aircraft manufacturer Embraer.
Who is credited with discovering Lynx?
Lynx (constellation): Johannes Hevelius. Lynx is a constellation named after the animal, usually observed in the Northern Celestial Hemisphere.
Who is credited with discovering Newton's law of universal gravitation?
Newton's law of universal gravitation: Robert Hooke. This is a general physical law derived from empirical observations by what Isaac Newton called inductive reasoning.
Who is credited with discovering Pulsar?
Pulsar: Jocelyn Bell Burnell. This produces a very precise interval between pulses that ranges from milliseconds to seconds for an individual pulsar.
Who is credited with discovering Coma Berenices?
Coma Berenices: Conon of Samos. Coma Berenices is an ancient asterism in the northern sky, which has been defined as one of the 88 modern constellations.

First coined as a term in 1852, this pattern of continued drinking despite its harms affected an estimated 283 million people worldwide as of 2016, according to the World Health Organization — name the condition?
Alcoholism is the continued drinking of alcohol despite the problems it causes.

Affecting roughly 1 in 15,000 people, this rare genetic disorder impairs the nervous system, causing severe intellectual disability and little to no speech, but is also linked to an unusually happy demeanor — what's it called?
Angelman syndrome (AS) is a rare genetic disorder that affects approximately 1 in 15,000 individuals.
This South Korean actress started as a child model in 2005 and later starred in the popular series True Beauty. Who is she?
Arrhythmia are irregularities in the heartbeat, including when it is too fast or too slow.
Nicknamed 'Red-Stockings,' this French herding dog breed hails from the plains of Central France — which breed is it?
Beauceron (French) is a herding dog breed originating from the plains of Central France.
Around 2,500 species of this insect family defend themselves by secreting a skin-irritating toxin called cantharidin, often flaunting bold warning colors — which family?
Blister beetle are beetles of the family Meloidae, so called for their defensive secretion of a blistering agent, cantharidin.

This British dog breed of mastiff type has a stocky build, a large head, thick facial skin folds, and a protruding lower jaw, and is now illegal to breed in the Netherlands over health concerns — name the breed?
Bulldog is a British breed of dog of mastiff type. It may also be known as the English Bulldog or British Bulldog.
Seen as the frontman of Mexican neoliberalism, this economist-president championed and signed NAFTA after an election clouded by fraud accusations — who is he?
Carlos Salinas de Gortari (Spanish; born 3 April 1948) is a Mexican economist and former politician who served as the 60th president of Mexico from 1988 to 1994.
Patented in 1948 and used to treat hay fever and other allergic conditions, this first-generation antihistamine works within two hours by blocking the H1 histamine receptor — name the drug?
Chlorphenamine (CP, CPM), also known as chlorpheniramine, is an antihistamine used to treat the symptoms of allergic conditions such as allergic rhinitis (hay fever).

Ranging across most of Europe and into the Palearctic as far as northwestern China, this medium-sized bird of prey sees its northernmost populations migrate as far as South Africa each winter — which raptor?
Common buzzard (Buteo buteo) is a medium-sized bird of prey with a large range.
Bottle gourds, bitter melon, and the fibrous fruit that gives us loofah sponges are all members of which roughly 965-species plant family?
Cucurbitaceae (kew-), also called cucurbits or the gourd family, are a plant family consisting of about 965 species in 101 genera.
Birds are the only surviving lineage of these warmblooded Mesozoic reptiles, having evolved from theropods in the Late Jurassic — what is the broader group called?
Dinosaur are a diverse group of warmblooded reptiles of the clade Dinosauria.
Discovered to have two undescribed relatives only in 2019, this Amazonian 'knifefish' is best known for generating powerful electric discharges — which species?
Electrophorus electricus is the best-known species of electric eel. It is considered as a freshwater teleost which contains an electrogenic tissue that produces electric discharges.
This Hungarian-American physicist won the 1963 Nobel for applying fundamental symmetry principles to the atomic nucleus, having once worked as an assistant to David Hilbert at Göttingen. Who was he?
Eugene Wigner (November 17, 1902 - January 1, 1995) was a Hungarian-American theoretical physicist who also contributed to mathematical physics.

This region of the upper limb, running between the elbow and the wrist, contains two long bones, the radius and the ulna, and is technically distinct from the 'arm' proper in anatomy — what is it called?
Forearm is the region of the upper limb between the elbow and the wrist. It is homologous to the region of the leg that lies between the knee and the ankle joints, the crus.

Sharing the 1988 Nobel Prize, this American biochemist pioneered rational drug design — studying a drug's target rather than relying on trial and error — and her work led to AZT, the first widely used AIDS drug. Who was she?
Gertrude B. Elion (January 23, 1918 - February 21, 1999) was an American biochemist and pharmacologist, who shared the 1988 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with George H. Hitchings.

Caused by a hormone imbalance between estrogens and androgens, this non-cancerous condition results in enlarged breast tissue in men and can occur in newborns, adolescents, and older or obese men — name the condition?

Gynecomastia (also spelled gynaecomastia) is the non-cancerous enlargement of one or both breasts in men due to the growth of breast tissue as a result of a hormone imbalance between estrogens and androgens.
With species ranging from evergreen trees to climbing shrubs across the tropics and temperate zones, this genus's most iconic species decorates Christmas cards worldwide — what genus is it?
Holly is a genus of over 570 species of flowering plants in the family Aquifoliaceae, and the only living genus in that family.

This nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug treats pain, fever, and inflammation — from migraines to arthritis — and typically starts working within an hour, whether taken orally or intravenously. What drug?
Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that is used to relieve pain, fever, and inflammation.

This American scientist co-authored a landmark 1953 paper with Francis Crick proposing the double-helix structure of DNA, building on research by Rosalind Franklin, and shared a 1962 Nobel Prize for the discovery — who is he?
James Watson (April 6, 1928 - November 6, 2025) was an American molecular biologist, geneticist, and zoologist.
Cousin to the wallaby and wallaroo in the family Macropodidae, this Australian marsupial's biggest member is the red one. What is it?
Kangaroo are marsupials from the subfamily Macropodinae (macropods, meaning "large foot").

Spread by the bite of sandflies and caused by a genus of protozoal parasites, this tropical disease can present as skin ulcers, disfiguring mucosal damage, or a more dangerous internal form. Name the disease?
Leishmaniasis is a wide array of clinical manifestations caused by protozoal parasites of the Trypanosomatida genus Leishmania.
Named for antennae often longer than its own body, this insect family boasts over 35,000 species and gets its name from a Greek myth about a shepherd transformed after angering nymphs — which group?
Longhorn beetle (Cerambycidae), also known as long-horned or longicorns (whose larvae are often referred to as roundheaded borers), are a large family of beetles, with over 35,000 species described.
This computer scientist led the on-board flight software for NASA's Apollo Guidance Computer and is credited with coining the very term 'software engineering' — who is she?
Margaret Hamilton (software engineer) (ne Heafield; born August 17, 1936) is an American computer scientist.
This field's founding body, the Bureau International des Poids et Mesures, grew out of an 1875 convention and eventually gave the world the International System of Units — what is this study called?
Metrology is the scientific study of measurement.
This small green legume, cultivated widely across East and South Asia, is used in both savory dishes and sweet desserts — what is it?
Mung bean (Vigna radiata) is a plant species in the legume family.
Born in the Austro-Hungarian Empire and emigrating to the US in 1884, he's known for pioneering the AC electricity system. Who?
Nikola Tesla (10 July 1856 - 7 January 1943) was a Serbian-American engineer, futurist, and inventor.
Chemists still debate the exact definition, but generally, any large molecule containing a carbon-hydrogen or carbon-carbon bond falls into this broad class of compounds. What is it?
Organic compound are a subclass of chemical compounds of carbon.

The males of this Phasianidae bird are famed for piercing calls and extravagant plumage; its Asiatic species include blue, green, and a third found only in the Congo Basin — what is this bird, collectively?

Peafowl is a common name for two bird species of the genus Pavo and one species of the closely related genus Afropavo within the tribe Pavonini of the family Phasianidae (the pheasants and their allies).

A pnictogen with only one stable isotope and atomic number 15, this element hides in Earth's crust mostly as phosphate rock and readily builds a vast family of organic and inorganic compounds. Which element is it?
Phosphorus is a chemical element; it has symbol P and atomic number 15.
Known as little hogweed or pursley, every part of this succulent plant can be eaten raw or cooked — what plant is it?
Portulaca oleracea (common purslane, also known as little hogweed, or pursley) is a succulent plant in the family Portulacaceae.
This kidney inflammation, most often caused by E. coli infection, typically causes fever and tenderness along the side of the body — what is it?
Pyelonephritis is inflammation of the kidney, typically due to a bacterial infection.
Also known as vitamin B2, this nutrient builds two key coenzymes for energy metabolism and may, taken orally, cut down on migraine headaches in adults — what is it?
Riboflavin is a vitamin found in food and sold as a dietary supplement.

This volatile, colorless, and odorless nerve agent is so potent a chemical weapon that inhaling a lethal dose can cause death from respiratory paralysis within one to ten minutes — what's the compound called?
Sarin (NATO designation GB short for G-series, B) is an extremely toxic organophosphorus compound that has been often used as a chemical weapon due to its extreme potency as a nerve agent.
Despite its long-nosed, mouse-like look, this small mammal is actually a closer cousin to hedgehogs and moles than to rodents — what is it?
Shrew (family Soricidae) are small mole-like mammals classified in the order Eulipotyphla.

This class of moisture-loving hexapods — the largest lineage of six-legged creatures excluded from the insect group — indirectly aids decomposition by breaking down organic matter and shaping soil microbial life. What are they?
Springtail (class Collembola) form the largest of the three lineages of modern hexapods that are no longer considered insects, the others being Protura and Diplura.

This genus of about a dozen woody flowering shrubs in the olive family, native from southeastern Europe to East Asia, is closely related to privet and provides food for several moth larvae — what is it commonly called?
Syringa is a genus of 12 currently recognized species of flowering woody plants in the olive family called lilacs.
This condition causes abnormally low platelet levels in the blood, leading to prolonged or excessive bleeding — what blood disorder is it?
Thrombocytopenia is a condition characterized by abnormally low levels of platelets (also known as thrombocytes) in the blood.
These large, heavyset American game birds have a distinctive fleshy growth called a snood hanging from the base of their beak, with wild and ocellated species. What birds are they?
Turkey (bird) are large, heavyset galliforms in the genus Meleagris, indigenous to the Americas.
An American investor and philanthropist, he is the chairman of Berkshire Hathaway and, as of January 2026, the ninth-richest person in the world. Who is he?
Warren Buffett (born August 30, 1930) is an American investor and philanthropist who is the chairman and former CEO of the conglomerate Berkshire Hathaway.
Also known as AZT, this was the very first antiretroviral drug used against HIV/AIDS, and can be given during birth to prevent mother-to-child spread — what is it?
Zidovudine (ZDV), also known as azidothymidine (AZT), was the first antiretroviral medication used to prevent and treat HIV/AIDS.
Nicknamed the cell's "molecular unit of currency," this energy-carrying molecule powers muscle contraction and nerve impulses, dropping to ADP or AMP when spent — what is it?
Adenosine triphosphate: Energy-carrying molecule in living cells.
This French surgeon won a 1912 Nobel for pioneering blood-vessel suturing and later teamed with aviator Charles Lindbergh to build an early perfusion pump for organ work. Who was he?
Alexis Carrel: French surgeon and biologist (1873–1944)
Domesticated in Southwest China roughly 2,000 years ago, this corm-producing plant is nicknamed 'devil's tongue' and gets boiled down into a jelly-like noodle called shirataki — what is it?
Amorphophallus konjac: Edible plant from Yunnan, China.
This self-taught Dutch draper turned lensmaker began exploring microbial life with his own single-lensed microscopes in the 1670s, earning him the title 'Father of Microbiology' — who was he?
This American psychiatrist and pharmaceutical marketer amassed the world's largest personal collection of Chinese art, later donated to the Smithsonian — who is he?
Arthur M. Sackler: American physician and executive (1913–1987)
Sold under the brand name Lioresal, this muscle relaxant treats spasticity from spinal cord injuries or MS and is sometimes used off-label for alcohol withdrawal — what is it?
Baclofen: Gabapentinoid and Skeletal Muscle Relaxant.

This steel-gray, brittle alkaline earth metal is found naturally only in combination with other elements, making up gemstones like aquamarine and emerald, and bonds so strongly to oxygen that extracting it is notoriously difficult — which element, atomic number 4?
Beryllium: Chemical element with atomic number 4 (Be)

Announced at the 1984 Farnborough Airshow and launched by Northwest Airlines, this advanced wide-body airliner added 6-foot winglets and a stretched upper deck to an already-famous jumbo jet design — which aircraft?
Boeing 747-400: Wide-body airliner, improved production series of the 747.

Branching from the windpipe at a landmark called the carina, these airway passages narrow progressively through several orders before losing cartilage support and changing name entirely — what are they called?
Bronchus: Airway in the respiratory tract.
Bearing distinctive fatty humps and used for milk, meat, and transport across deserts for millennia, which ungulate comes in a common one-humped form and a rarer two-humped form?
Its raw shell and seed are actually toxic until roasted or steamed, and the tropical American tree it grows on also yields a fleshy 'apple' — what is this familiar snack?
Cashew: Flowering plant in the family Anacardiaceae.
Also known as christophine or mirliton, this gourd-family fruit was first cultivated in Mesoamerica and is often cooked like summer squash — what is it?
Chayote: Edible fruiting vine of the gourd family.

An American naturalist who surveyed wildlife in Labrador, he turned his observations into quick-freezing methods that launched the modern frozen food industry — and a famous brand bears his name. Who was he?
Clarence Birdseye: American inventor, entrepreneur, and naturalist.

Though its wild populations are considered vulnerable to extinction, this domesticated freshwater fish has been introduced so widely that it's listed among the world's 100 worst invasive species — what is it?
Common carp: Species of fish. It gives its name to the carp family, Cyprinidae.
Spread mainly through the fecal-oral route, these single-stranded RNA enteroviruses share traits with poliovirus and rank among the leading causes of aseptic meningitis — which pathogens?
Coxsackievirus: Virus that causes digestive upset and sometimes heart damage.
This Harvard-trained legal scholar who wrote on criminal punishment and retribution joined Florida State's faculty in 2005, and was later murdered in a plot tied to his ex-wife's family — who is he?
Dan Markel: American law professor and murder victim (1972–2014)
This colorless, highly flammable liquid with a sweet smell was once widely used as a general anesthetic before modern alternatives — what compound?
After co-founding a social media giant, this entrepreneur left in 2008 to launch the workplace software company Asana — who is he?
Nicknamed the ALX, this Brazilian turboprop light-attack aircraft is assembled in Jacksonville, Florida with an American defense partner for low-threat counter-insurgency missions — which aircraft?
Embraer EMB 314 Super Tucano: Light ground attack and training aircraft.
Odorless, colorless, and dangerously sweet-tasting, this viscous compound goes into polyester fibers and antifreeze — and has even been spotted in outer space. What is it?
This principle describes how a changing magnetic field generates an electric current, underpinning the operation of transformers, generators, and motors — what is it called?
Faraday's law of induction: Basic law of electromagnetism.
Originally focused on water, this branch of physics studies liquids, gases, and plasmas, with applications from geophysics to aerospace engineering — which field?
Fluid mechanics: Branch of physics. Fluid mechanics is the branch of physics concerned with the mechanics of fluids (liquids, gases, and plasmas) and the forces on them.
Bound together by gravity, this vast system of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter can range from a dwarf with under a thousand stars to a supergiant with a hundred trillion — what is it?
Galaxy: System of stars and interstellar matter. The word is derived from the Greek galaxias (γαλαξίας), meaning 'milky', a reference to the Milky Way galaxy that contains the Solar System.

Likely first domesticated by Austronesian peoples in Maritime Southeast Asia, this herbaceous perennial is grown for the spicy rhizome that puts it in the same family as turmeric and cardamom — what is it?
Ginger: Species of plant used as a spice.
Also known as the Congo variety, this African bird in the family Psittacidae lost its old 'African' nickname once a related Timneh species was split off as its own species — what is it?
Grown as deciduous shrubs across the temperate Northern Hemisphere and related to the birch family, this plant produces a popular round brown nut — which plant genus?
Discovered in 1910 and stored in mast cells and basophils, this compound triggers immune responses and doubles as a neurotransmitter in the brain, spinal cord, and uterus — what is it?
Histamine: Organic compound involved in immune responses.
Teaching philosophy and astronomy in Roman-era Alexandria, this Neoplatonist is considered the first female mathematician whose life is well documented — who is she?
Sitting on the electromagnetic spectrum between visible light and microwaves, this invisible radiation makes up most of the black-body glow given off by objects near room temperature — what is it?

Infrared: Form of electromagnetic radiation. Infrared (IR; sometimes called infrared light) is electromagnetic radiation (EMR) with wavelengths longer than that of visible light but shorter than microwaves.
Working under Tamerlane around 1400, this Persian astronomer and mathematician produced work that mostly never reached Europe and stays largely unpublished — who is it?
Jamshid al-Kashi: Persian astronomer and mathematician (c. 1380–1429)
Before flying on Space Shuttle mission STS-128 in 2009, this Mexican-American engineer helped develop digital mammography equipment at Lawrence Livermore — who is he?
José M. Hernández: American engineer, vintner, and former NASA astronaut.
Bred for their dazzling colors since the early 19th century in Niigata, Japan, these ornamental carp come in patterns like Kōhaku and Shōwa Sanshoku — what are they?
Koi: Colored varieties of Amur carp.

This small wild feline of South and Southeast Asia sports dark spots on a tawny coat and two stripes running from its eyes to its ears, and can live as high as 4,474 meters in the Himalayas — what is it?
Leopard cat: Small wild cat species. The leopard cat (Prionailurus bengalensis) is a small wild cat with dark spots on the tawny-coloured body and limbs.

Developed under the US Air Force's Advanced Tactical Fighter program, this American twin-engine stealth fighter was designed for air superiority but also handles ground attack, electronic warfare and signals intelligence — which aircraft?

Lockheed Martin F-22 Raptor: American stealth air superiority fighter. The Lockheed Martin–Boeing F-22 Raptor is an American twin-engine, jet-powered, all-weather, supersonic stealth fighter aircraft.
Element number 12 is so eager to ignite that, once lit, it burns with a brilliant-white light — this lightweight alkaline-earth metal, less dense than aluminium, is what?
Magnesium: Chemical element with atomic number 12 (Mg)
Part of the chamomile tribe within the sunflower family, some species in this plant genus share the common name 'mayweed' — which genus?
Discovered in 1893 and existing as two mirror-image enantiomers, this CNS stimulant is best known in its hydrochloride-salt form nicknamed 'crystal' — what is it?

Also called 'selective sound sensitivity syndrome,' this disorder causes specific sounds to trigger strong negative emotional and physiological reactions, though it isn't yet listed in the DSM-5-TR — what is it called?
Misophonia: Disorder of decreased tolerance to specific sounds.

Grouping over 30 inherited disorders that cause progressive weakening and wasting of skeletal tissue — with the Duchenne form affecting roughly half of all cases in young boys — what's this disease group called?
Muscular dystrophy: Diseases in which skeletal and visceral muscles break down over time.

First arising in wormlike organisms 550 to 600 million years ago, this body-wide network splits into a central hub of brain and spinal cord and a peripheral web of nerve fibers relaying signals to and from every body part — which network?
Nervous system: Part of an animal that coordinates actions and senses.

This healthcare profession blends the art and science of caring, focusing on protecting and promoting health, preventing illness, and easing suffering through compassionate, hands-on care — what field is it?
Nursing: Health care profession. Nurses may help coordinate care performed by other providers or act independently as nursing professionals.
Named from Greek words meaning 'porous bones,' this disorder causes bone density loss serious enough that fractures can occur with minor stress, especially in the elderly — what is it?
Osteoporosis: Skeletal disorder. Osteoporosis is the most common reason for a broken bone among the elderly.
Also known as trisomy 13, this chromosomal condition arises when cells carry extra genetic material from chromosome 13, causing widespread organ defects — which syndrome?
Patau syndrome: Chromosomal disorder in which there are three copies of chromosome 13.
Its Nahuatl name means 'caterpillar cocoon,' but this spineless desert cactus is better known for containing the psychoactive alkaloid mescaline — what is it?
Peyote: Species of psychoactive cactus. Peyote, also known as Lophophora williamsii, is a small, spineless cactus which contains psychoactive alkaloids, particularly mescaline.

A member of the cashew family, this tree nut is a priority allergen, yet the world still churned out 1.4 million tonnes in 2024 — with the US, Iran, and Turkey making up 87% of it. Which green-hued nut is it?
Pistachio: Member of the cashew family. The pistachio (UK also; Pistacia vera) is a small to medium-sized tree of the cashew family.
This imperial unit of pressure equals about 6.895 kilopascals and is the number you check when filling a bicycle tire to around 65 — which unit?
Pound per square inch: Unit of pressure or stress. It is the pressure resulting from a force with magnitude of one pound-force applied to an area of one square inch.

Described as 'the translation of politics into the reality that citizens experience every day,' this field implements government policies and programs to solve social and economic problems — what is it called?
Public administration: Academic discipline; implementation or management of policy.
Native to the southern United States, this pond terrapin is the world's most commonly traded and most invasive turtle, largely due to pet releases — which species?
This American neuroscientist and primatologist, a Stanford professor across three departments, has spent his career studying the neuroendocrinology of stress — who is he?
The largest genus in the mint family, this group of nearly 1,000 shrubs and herbs includes common cooking sage and rosemary — what's the genus called?
Salvia: Largest genus of plants in the mint family. Salvia is the largest genus of plants in the sage family Lamiaceae, with just under 1,000 species of shrubs, herbaceous perennials, and annuals.
A peptide mimicking a gut hormone, this drug treats type 2 diabetes as Ozempic and Rybelsus but is sold as Wegovy for weight loss — what's the underlying medication?
Related to polecats but more closely kin to the Old World stink badgers, these black-and-white mammals defend themselves by spraying a foul-smelling liquid from their anal glands — which animal?
Skunk: Common name of mammals in the family Mephitidae.
Acting as a blood filter and red-blood-cell recycling center, which vertebrate organ also stores a reserve of blood for use during hemorrhagic shock?
Spleen: Immune organ that filters blood.
